p.challenge: Locker 9: find every rectangle array of 9 stars. Each one is a factor pair = visitors who flip locker 9. 3 × 3 uses one number twice, so 9 has an odd number of factors (1, 3, 9). Flipped 3 times, it stays open!

p.label: tiles
p.challenge: Each new L of tiles is the next odd number: 1, 3, 5, 7, ... How many tiles are in square 15? That is the sum of the first 15 odd numbers.

p.title: Can it be a perfect square?

nodes.info: A square can only end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.
Units digit of a square: 1 or 9 → 1; 2 or 8 → 4; 3 or 7 → 9; 4 or 6 → 6; 5 → 5; 0 → 0.
2, 3, 7 and 8 never appear as the last digit of a square.

nodes.text: An odd number of 0s at the end?
nodes.info: If a number ends in k zeros, its square ends in 2k zeros — always an even number of zeros.
4,000 ends in 3 zeros. A square always ends in an even number of zeros.
Passing the tests does not prove it: 26 ends in 6 but is not a square. 841 is: 29² = 841.

p.challenge: Test a number with the square clues: choose Yes or No at each question. Play again to reach every ending.

p.label: gap
p.challenge: Gaps between neighbouring squares: 4 − 1 = 3, 9 − 4 = 5, 16 − 9 = 7, ... Gap n is n + (n + 1). Which gap number is 25? (It is the gap from n² up to (n + 1)².)
49 < 50 < 64, so √50 lies between 7 and 8, closer to 7. Drag the frog to √50 correct to one decimal place (check: 7.1² = 50.41).
Square-root game: √4489. 60² = 3600 < 4489 < 4900 = 70², so the root is in the 60s. 4489 ends in 9, so the root ends in 3 or 7. 65² = 4225 < 4489. Drag the frog to √4489.

p.title: Cube root of 343

nodes.info: 343 is odd and does not end in 0 or 5, so try 7.
7 divides 343.
7 divides again — and 7 is prime.
The primes make one group of three equal primes.

p.challenge: Put the steps in order to find ∛343 by grouping prime factors in threes.
Cubing keeps the sign: (−3)³ = (−3) × (−3) × (−3). Drag the frog to (−3)³. (Its last digit 7 matches 3³ = 27.)

p.label: second difference
p.challenge: Cubes 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216 have gaps 7, 19, 37, 61, 91. The gaps of those gaps go 12, 18, 24, 30 (up 6 each time). Find the 5th one — then 91 + it gives 7³ − 6³.

p.title: Make 500 a perfect cube

nodes.info: 5 × 5 × 5 is a full group. 2 × 2 is one 2 short of a group.
Choose one way, then come back and try the other.
Removing the leftover 2 × 2 leaves 5³.
Every prime now appears a multiple of 3 times.

p.challenge: 500 is not a perfect cube. Press Next, then choose: multiply or divide to turn it into one. Try both ways!

p.title: Squares, cubes and roots in history
p.challenge: Put these moments in the history of squares, cubes and roots in time order — oldest on top.

events.label: Babylonian tablets of squares and cubes
events.info: Scribes made clay tablets listing squares and cubes to speed up calculations.

events.label: Aryabhata describes varga (square)
events.info: Varga: a square figure with four equal sides, and the product of two equal numbers.

events.label: Brahmagupta gives rules for squares and square roots
events.info: Written in his book Brahmasphutasiddhanta (7th century CE).

events.label: Al-Khwarizmi writes jidhr for root in Arabic
events.info: Around 820 CE in Baghdad. The Indian idea of mula (root of a plant) travelled into Arabic as jidhr, and later into Latin as radix.

p.label: layers
p.challenge: Each paper fold doubles the layers: 2, 4, 8, ... (2ⁿ after n folds). How many layers after 10 folds? Compare 2¹⁰ with 10² = 100!

p.title: Doubling vs adding 2
p.challenge: Both rows start 2, 4. The orange bars add 2 each step (linear). Change the purple bars so each one DOUBLES (exponential). Which grows faster?

p.title: Which law of exponents?
p.challenge: Look at the bases and the exponents. Which law simplifies each one? Sort them all, then press Check.

p.title: Work out 8⁴ ÷ 4⁵

nodes.info: Both 8 and 4 are powers of 2.
Replace each base.
Power of a power: multiply the exponents.
Same base, divide: subtract the exponents.

p.challenge: Put the steps in order to work out 8⁴ ÷ 4⁵ by changing the bases to match.
3 shirts and 4 pants: each row is a shirt, each column is a pair of pants. Build the array of every outfit — how many are there?
Power line of 4: each number is an exponent (4⁻², 4⁻¹, 4⁰ = 1, 4¹, 4², 4³). Start at 4². Dividing by 4³ means 3 steps left. Where do you land — and what is that power of 4?
Build the number 4 × 10³ + 7 × 10² + 0 × 10¹ + 5 × 10⁰ on the abacus.
Build 4,50,000. Then imagine moving the decimal point left until one digit is in front: 4.5 — 5 jumps, so 4,50,000 = 4.5 × 10⁵.

nodes.info: Guess first — maybe a few thousand coins?

Does the answer make sense? Compare it with your guess.

p.title: Which power is which?

p.title: Counting goats with pebbles

The goats graze in the fields all day.
In the evening, one pebble is taken back for each goat that returns.
Pebbles are left over — so some goats are missing!

events.label: Aryabhata explains place value

events.label: Al-Khwarizmi writes on Indian numerals in Baghdad
events.info: Around 825 CE (9th century). Al-Khwarizmi and Al-Kindi wrote books on calculating with Indian numerals.

events.label: Fibonacci's Liber Abaci
events.info: This book spread the Indian numerals across Europe.

events.label: The Bakhshali manuscript is found

p.title: A herder's tally (bundles of 5)

p.label: landmark
p.challenge: Base-5 landmarks: 1, 5, 25, 125, ... each 5 times the one before. 25 × 125 = 5² × 5³ = 5⁵. Which landmark is that? (Term 6 is 5⁵.)
In base 2 the places are 8, 4, 2, 1 and the only digits are 0 and 1. Spin the wheels to write eleven and then thirteen in base 2.
Base 60 lives on in clocks! The Babylonian number '2 | 15' means 2 × 60 + 15 = 135. Move the hands 135 minutes forward from 1:00.

p.title: The big story of number systems

nodes.info: One mark or pebble for each object.
Bundling tally marks, for example in fives.
Like the Egyptian heel bone for 10 and coiled rope for 100.

nodes.text: Landmarks as powers of a base

A digit’s value depends on its position.

p.challenge: Arrange the big story of numbers, from the first tallies to zero.

Diagonal AC goes from (−4, 0) to (4, 0). Plot D so that the diagonals AC and BD bisect each other at right angles but are not equal. Which quadrilateral is ABCD?
A quadrilateral has angles 70°, 80° and 95°. All four angles add to 360° (a diagonal makes two triangles: 180° + 180°). Make the fourth angle.
In parallelogram ABCD, neighbouring angles add up to 180°. If ∠A = 70°, make ∠B as angle 2 — angle 1 should then show 70°.
Two congruent triangles, each with base 6 and height 4 (area 12), are joined with one turned half-way round. They make a parallelogram! Build it: base 6, height 4, area 24.
Trapezium ABCD has AB ∥ DC, and side AD cuts across them like a transversal. Co-interior angles add to 180° (∠A + ∠D = 180°). Make ∠6 = 115° and read its co-interior partner.

p.title: From any quadrilateral to a square
p.challenge: Every square is a rhombus, every rhombus is a parallelogram, every parallelogram is a quadrilateral. Order the family from the most general to the most special, using the diagonals.

p.challenge: Triangular numbers are 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1) ÷ 2. How many dots are in triangle 10?
Roll two dice and add. Even + even = even, odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd. Predict P(even total), then roll to check.
13 leaves remainder 3 and 9 leaves remainder 4 when shared among 5. Share 13 + 9 = 22 among 5 plates. The remainders add: 3 + 4 = 7 = one more 5 and 2. What is left over?
Pebble riddle: the number is 1 more than a multiple of 60 (the LCM of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6). Hop by 60 from 1 and stop at the first number that 7 divides exactly.
9,100 is a multiple of 4 (because 100 is). Hop in 4s from 9,100 to the last multiple of 4 below 9,147. 9,147 is 3 more — the same remainder as 47 ÷ 4!

p.title: Digital root of 9,875

Keep going until one digit is left.
The digital root is 2.

p.title: Crack EF × E = GGG

nodes.info: A number like 777 is 7 × 111.

Every letter is now a digit: E = 3, F = 7, G = 1.

p.challenge: Arrange the clues in order to crack the letter puzzle EF × E = GGG.
6 × 4 = 24. Add 1 to the 6: (6 + 1) × 4 = 24 + 4. Drag the corner to make 7 × 4 and see the area grow by exactly 4, the other factor.
Build 6 rows of 12 stars. Split each row into 10 + 2: 6 × 12 = 6 × 10 + 6 × 2 = 60 + 12. Is the total 72?

p.title: Grid method: (x² + 2x + 3)(x + 1)

nodes.text: Fill all 6 boxes: x³, 2x², 3x and x², 2x, 3
nodes.info: Each box = its row term × its column term. 3 × 2 = 6 products.
Only like terms can be added.
The finished product.

p.challenge: Put the grid-method steps in order to multiply (x² + 2x + 3)(x + 1).

Make an L-shape: a 7 × 7 square with a 3 × 3 corner cut out. Its area is 7² − 3². Cut it into two rectangles and line them up: (7 + 3) × (7 − 3). Both give 40!

p.title: Why the calendar trick always gives 7

nodes.text: Pick a 2 × 2 block: top row a, a + 1

The date below is 7 more (one week later).

nodes.text: Multiply across the diagonals: (a + 1)(a + 7) and a(a + 8)

nodes.info: Expand with the distributive property.
a² + 8a + 7 − (a² + 8a) = 7, whatever a is.

p.challenge: Arrange the steps of the proof of the calendar trick.
A 6 cm × 4 cm photo is enlarged so it still looks alike: BOTH sides are multiplied by 2. Drag the corner to make the enlarged photo.

Is 3 : 4 :: 12 : 16? Cut the bottom bar into 16 parts and shade as much as 3/4. If you need exactly 12 parts, it is a proportion (3 × 16 = 4 × 12 = 48).
5 kg of apples cost ₹600, so 1 kg costs ₹600 ÷ 5. Pay the exact price of 8 kg of apples.

A 5 cm × 5 cm square has area 25. Make the length 20% longer (6 cm) and the breadth 20% shorter (4 cm). Is the area the same? 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, so it falls by 4%!

Plot a point with whole-number coordinates exactly 13 units from O. Its x, its y and 13 form a Pythagorean triple — and it is not a multiple of (3, 4, 5)!

nodes.info: The stem stays the same length when it bends.
Depth and distance are the legs; the stem is the hypotenuse.
Expand (d + 10)².
Take d² and 100 from both sides.
The water is 40 cm deep, and the stem is 50 cm.
